key_idea: An L1 bisector with dx>dy is a curve x=clamp(+-y+c, lo, hi) (dx<dy: the same with axes swapped; dx=dy contains quadrants and meets everything), so only same-orientation pairs can miss each other, and that reduces to interval-disjointness plus a 3D dominance count.
sketch: Work in doubled coordinates. Curves of different orientation always cross, and a dx=dy bisector contains a curve of each orientation, so count non-intersecting pairs only among x=f(y) curves and among y=g(x) curves. Two such curves are disjoint iff their value ranges [lo,hi] are disjoint, or they have the same strict monotonicity and c1<c2, lo1<lo2, hi1<hi2 (opposite monotonicity or a straight line needs disjoint ranges). So non-intersecting = #range-disjoint pairs (sort + binary search) + per monotone class [#(c1<c2,lo1<lo2,hi1<hi2) - #(c1<c2,hi1<lo2)], the first by CDQ divide and conquer with a Fenwick tree and the second by a sorted sweep; the answer is C(n,2) minus that. O(n log^2 n), 0.2 s for n=1.5e5. Pitfalls: strict inequalities with ties (sort equal c by lo descending so CDQ never counts them), the area-shaped dx=dy bisectors, dx=0 or dy=0 lines, and a 64-bit answer. Stress-tested on 1500 random small cases against a quarter-lattice brute force.
